podcast.title: "How Sweet and Idiot" Sketch (1973)
podcast.body: Members of this comedy troupe sued Oasis, claiming that Oasis's song "Shaker Maker" sounded very similar to a song featured in their 1973 TV sketch titled "How Sweet and Idiot." "They insisted that Shaker Maker sounded a lot like a song from a 1973 TV sketch called How Sweet and Idiot."

podcast.title: Theme Song from "Flying Circus" (Year not specified)
podcast.body: The theme song for Monty Python's Flying Circus is actually John Philip Sousa's march, "The Liberty Bell," composed in 1893. This association made the military march widely recognizable to a new generation. "So, yeah, that's the theme from Monty Python's Flying Circus, but it's actually a march composed in 1893 by American John Philip Susa."

xref.title: Early Bands (High School)
xref.body: Before forming The Trews, Colin McDonald played in "not serious" punk and grunge bands with friends in high school while living in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. His first band with a buddy from grade nine was called "One-eyed Trouser Snake," inspired by Monty Python's "Meaning of Life." "I started playing in like not serious like kind of punk and grunge bands in high school with my friends."

xref.title: First Canadian Band to Sign to Stiff Records – Power Pop Side of Vancouver Punk
xref.body: The Pointed Sticks formed in Vancouver in 1978, five former members overlapping with D.O.A. and the Subhumans. Their sound was more melodic and power pop-leaning than their contemporaries — five members singing harmonies was unusual in punk. Their name came from a Monty Python sketch about self-defense against pointed sticks. They became the first Canadian band to sign to Stiff Records in the UK, home to the Damned, Nick Lowe, Elvis Costello, and Ian Dury. Several strong singles and one album followed. Their relative accessibility broadened the audience for Vancouver punk. "Stiff Records, one of the groundbreaking indie labels in the UK."

xref.title: Funding for "Monty Python and the Holy Grail"
xref.body: The significant earnings from Pink Floyd's "Dark Side of the Moon" album provided crucial financial support for the production of the film "Monty Python and the Holy Grail." The band members, who enjoyed watching Monty Python on the BBC during recording breaks, donated £200,000 to the Pythons after learning of their funding difficulties, and also encouraged Led Zeppelin and Genesis to contribute. "When they were working on the record, the band would relax by watching Monty Python on the BBC. When they heard that the pythons were struggling to make the movie, they sent Python a check for two hundred thousand pounds."

xref.body: Terry Gilliam, known for his work with Monty Python, was interested in a Gorillaz movie project during the "Demon Days" era, though the film was never made. "Monty Python Man Terry Gilliam was interested. There was even a working title. Bananas spelled with a Z, of course."

xref.title: Later Pursuits and Companies
xref.body: In the 1990s, Bob Ezrin diversified his career by founding Seventh Level Incorporated, an interactive multimedia company responsible for titles like the Monty Python CD-ROM "A Complete Waste of Time" and the children's series "Great Adventure" with Jaime Mandel. He also operates a recording facility called Enigma Digital. "Bob moved on to other pursuits in the 1990s. He founded an interactive multimedia company called Seventh Level Incorporated."

xref.title: Original Name: One-eyed Trouser Snake
xref.body: Before becoming The Trews, Colin McDonald had a punk/grunge band in high school in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia with a friend who shared a love for Monty Python. This earlier band was named One-eyed Trouser Snake, after a song from Monty Python's "Meaning of Life." When the core members (Colin, John Angus, Jack) formed, they adopted a shortened version, "One-eyed Trouser." "me and my buddy from grade nine really liked Monty Python and we called our first band One-eyed trouser snake from that song from Meaning of Life."

xref.title: Shaker Maker Lawsuit (Monty Python)
xref.body: In addition to The New Seekers, Oasis faced a second lawsuit over "Shaker Maker" from members of Monty Python's Flying Circus. They claimed the song sounded strikingly similar to a song from their 1973 TV sketch "How Sweet and Idiot." "Oasis was also sued by, wait for it, members of Monty Python's Flying Circus. They insisted that Shaker Maker sounded a lot like a song from a 1973 TV sketch called How Sweet and Idiot."
